tier_reason: The HN Ask post (item 31796311, 2022-06-19) does list GET/SET ops/sec for Redis 112,100/99,892 and Skytable 619,992/676,091 at 30 threads x 1 client on 2x m5.4xlarge. It is not a well-known benchmark suite: it is one post by an anonymous account, with no payload size, no server versions, no statement of which tool produced which number, and no scripts. Commenters asked for the missing methodology. So these are numbers without methodology, which is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: GET/SET ops/sec (30 threads, 1 client per thread): Skytable 619,992/676,091 vs Redis 112,100/99,892, about 5.5x GET and 6.8x SET (derived from page data); KeyDB 288,931/282,997 and Dragonfly 408,322/392,446 in the same post
corrections.caveats: The post does NOT state that the benchmarker has no affiliation, and its independence is doubtful. The HN account johnwoods also submitted 'Skytable - A realtime NoSQL Database written in Rust' (2022-08-26), 'Skytable NoSQL Database: Even with BlueQL, Skytable Outperforms Redis and KeyDB' (2023-12-05, linking ohsayan/sky-benches) and 'Skytable's new NoSQL engine released' (2023-12-09). The post gives no payload size, server versions, build flags or scripts, and does not say which of redis-benchmark/memtier/sky-bench produced the table. The author says Skytable was 'a little inconsistent at times' and that they could not reproduce Dragonfly's claimed 25x. Dragonfly's author replied in the thread with his own m5.4xlarge memtier run (about 1.02M SET ops/s at 28 threads x 20 connections), and the poster objected to the differing connection count. The numbers are from June 2022, before Skytable 0.8 moved to BlueQL. Skytable's own sky-benches repo (first-party, chart only, Tiger Lake 6C/12T, no compiler or flags) is not stronger evidence.

notes: I downgraded B to C: an anonymous HN post with no methodology does not count as an independent third-party suite, and the poster's history is heavily Skytable-promotional. The record's 'states no affiliation' claim was unsupported, so I rewrote the caveats. I read the HN item through the Algolia items API mirror. The repo metadata matches: AGPL-3.0, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-26.

tier_reason: Momento's blog (Khawaja Shams, 2025-05-07) is independent of the Valkey project and runs Valkey 8.1.1 against Redis 8.0 on the same c8g.2xlarge. It gives the exact docker and valkey-benchmark commands and states 999.8K vs 729.4K SET RPS, '37% higher on SET and 16% higher on GET', and 30%/60%+ faster p99. It falls short of A because the servers are official Docker images with unstated compiler/flags, and no benchmark repo is linked. B follows the batch-39 precedent that an independent vendor blog counts as B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Valkey 8.1.1 999.8K RPS on SET at 0.8ms p99 vs Redis 8.0 729.4K RPS on SET at 0.99ms p99. The page itself states '37% higher on SET and 16% higher on GET, alongside 30% faster p99 latencies for SET and 60%+ faster on GET' (these are stated, not derived). Absolute GET RPS is not printed in the text.
corrections.workload: valkey-benchmark -t SET,GET -r 3000000 -d 1024 --threads 6: each iteration is 50M SETs followed by 50M GETs, with 1KB values and a 3M-key keyspace. Connection count was tuned per system: Valkey peaked at 400 connections, Redis at 384. Both servers ran in Docker with --io-threads 6 and persistence off (--save '' --appendonly no), pinned to 6 cores with NIC IRQs pinned to the other 2.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Official Docker images valkey/valkey:8.1.1 and redis:8.0, run with --io-threads 6 --save '' --appendonly no --maxmemory 10gb; client was valkey-benchmark with --threads 6. Compiler/build flags of the images are not stated.

notes: I verified every figure on the page. One small fix: the 16%/60%+ figures are printed on the page, not derived. The page's headline has a typo, 'Redis 8.0 got as high as 729.4 RPS'; the connection-tuning section confirms 729.4K. Valkey is a hard fork of Redis per its README (GitHub fork flag false), so I set is_fork_of. Metadata matches: BSD-3-Clause, 27,299 stars, last commit 2026-09-26. The author is at Momento, which sells Valkey-based services, so the tier holds only if interested-vendor blogs count as B; otherwise it is C.

tier_reason: EloqData's own blog (2024-08-17, Wayback 2026-06-16) runs EloqKV 0.7.4 against Redis 7.2.5 and DragonflyDB 1.21.2 on c7g.8xlarge with full memtier commands. It says both 'significantly outperform Redis', with throughput and P999 shown only in chart images. The numbers are first-party, and no compiler, flags or CPU model beyond the instance type are given, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Text: 'EloqKV and DragonflyDB both outperform Redis due to their support for multiple worker threads' and 'both significantly outperform Redis, both in throughput and in latency'. The chart images (read by eye, approximate) show Redis flat at about 200 KOps at every concurrency. EloqKV is about 950 KOps at 128 connections, about 1,400 at 256, and about 1,600-1,700 at 512-1024, roughly 4.5-8.5x Redis. Redis P999 reaches about 11-12 ms at 1024 connections vs about 3 ms for EloqKV. DragonflyDB is slightly ahead of EloqKV throughout.
corrections.caveats: This is a first-party benchmark by EloqData, the company behind EloqKV, not an independent third party. The live URL eloqdata.com/blog/2024/08/17/benchmark-single-node returns HTTP 404 and www.eloqdata.com did not connect as of 2026-09-26; the content comes from a Wayback snapshot dated 2026-06-16. Redis was started as 'redis-server --save "" --appendonly no' with no --io-threads, so single-threaded Redis was compared against multi-threaded servers on a 32-vCPU box. The page itself concedes that Redis would normally be scaled out as a cluster. No compiler or build flags are given for any server. The README cites 'up to 1.6M QPS on AWS c6g.8xlarge' while the blog used c7g.8xlarge. License: the eloqkv repo (the Redis API layer) is dual GPLv2 or AGPLv3 with no 'or later' in LICENSE or the source headers. Its required core submodule eloqdata/tx_service (Data Substrate) is under the Business Source License 2.0 (non-OSI; Change Date 2031-01-08 to Apache-2.0), so a full build is not all-OSI.

notes: Tier C and the claim hold. I corrected the license from '-or-later' to '-only' per the LICENSE and file headers. I changed usability to 'mixed' because the tx_service core submodule is BSL. I read approximate values off the three archived chart images. Metadata matches: 1,501 stars, last commit 2026-09-17, not a fork, not archived.
